The challenges to be met are these:

  • Use the same memory mappings for all privilege levels. (This prevents TLB flushes which kill performance.)

  • Allow speculative execution.

  • Allow speculative execution across privilege changes.

  • Detect and stall when speculative execution violates memory privileges.

  • Detect this with no table lookups or address decoding. (For speed. The privilege checks will occur inside pipeline stages, so any delay kills the clock speed.)

Solution:

Divide the virtual memory addresses into privilege selector bits and index bits.

For example:

Privilege selector bits [63:56] Index bits [55:0]
PPPPPPPP AAA ... AAA

Only one selector bit will be set to one. The others will be cleared to zero. Which one is set to one will determine the privilege level needed to access that memory mapping.

Access will be validated by a privilege mask. If any bit is set in both the privilege mask and the selector bits, speculative execution is allowed. This will be very fast, since it uses only AND gates followed by an OR gate.

For example:

P bits Privilege mask Privilege level
00000001 11111111 Internal processor functions
00000010 11111110 System management mode
00000100 11111100 Hypervisor ring 1
00001000 11111000 Hypervisor ring 2
00010000 11110000 Hypervisor ring 3
00100000 11100000 Guest ring 1
01000000 11000000 Guest ring 2
10000000 10000000 Guest ring 3

More bits can be added to provide more isolation levels. Privilege masks can omit less-privileged memory mappings to create a special management task that cannot snoop.

Privilege levels are used to separate one program from the infrastructure that supports it. A program can make a lot of accesses to the infrastructure, so we have to make privilege changes efficient. That's what my article is about.

To change between programs we clear out everything and start from scratch with the new program. The new program has the same privilege level as the old one, but the memory mappings are changed.

Here's an analogy with hotels. Privilege changes are like calling room service. You can't cook something in the kitchen yourself, so you call on someone to do it for you. The call needs to be fast, because you don't want to wait. Program changes are like when you check out and a new guest checks in. It takes a long time for you to pack and the next guest to unpack. And then the next guest needs the same fast, efficient calls to room service, billed to their own account.

Do modern processors clear their entire cache memory every time the operating system decides it's time to switch to a new process? I don't think so, and if they don't then your analogy does not apply, you will still need a mask for each and every virtualized container.

A privilege level is not a vault that a process is locked inside. It is the current status of the current process, and the status required to access a resource. It is like the colored name badges that some companies use. Black and yellow stripes means a visitor who must be escorted everywhere. Green means an employee who can go into rooms with green labels. Blue means an executive who can go everywhere.

Privilege levels are reused when the OS switches to a new process. When a task switch occurs, the new process's registers are loaded into the processor. One of the registers is a control register that says what the process's current privilege level is.

Things are generally set up so that user code has a privilege level that barely lets it do anything. When user code makes a system call, its privilege level is changed and it jumps to OS code. The new privilege level generally lets the process do anything. But since the process is running carefully written OS code this is OK. When the OS code finishes, it restores the old privilege level and returns to user code.

The container systems you are talking about appear to be a kernel extension that merely wraps a layer of isolation around the system calls. Unix OSes for years now have had chroot jails that try to isolate processes from each other, but the isolation has been pretty weak. It appears that these containers intercept the system calls and virtualize everything. However each container is just a group of processes running normally. The container service just keeps them from seeing anything outside except by using networking.
